questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Point on a Line That Is Closest to a Given Point
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13934287/assets/f97972b1765e58a76475a99a97e4a8818b05efa1f26a79a232b250b6ef681e9b.png)

Find the point on the line $2y-3x=3$ that is closest to the point $(2,-2).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the equation of the given line in slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}2y-3x & =3 \\ 2y & =3x+3 \\ y & =\frac{3}{2}x+\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the equation of the line that's perpendicular to $y=\frac{3}{2}x+\frac{3}{2}$ and passes through the point $(2,-2).$

 The given line has a slope of $\frac{3}{2},$ so our perpendicular line must have a slope of $-\frac{2}{3}.$

Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the perpendicular line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y+2 & =-\frac{2}{3}(x-2) \\ y+2 & =-\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{4}{3} \\ y & =-\frac{2}{3}x-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We now find the point where the two lines intersect. To do this, we solve the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=\frac{3}{2}x+\frac{3}{2} \\ y=-\frac{2}{3}x-\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this system by putting the two equations equal to one another and solving for $x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}x+\frac{3}{2} & =-\frac{2}{3}x-\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{3}{2}x+\frac{2}{3}x & =-\frac{3}{2}-\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{13}{6}x & =-\frac{13}{6} \\ x & =-\frac{6}{13}\cdot \frac{13}{6} \\ x & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=-1$ into either of the two equations gives $y=0.$ So, our solution is $x=-1$ and $y=0.$ So, the lines intersect at the point $(-1,0).$

Therefore, we conclude that the point on the line $2y-3x=3$ that is closest to the point $(2,-2)$ is  $(-1,0).$

Find the point on the line $y+x=-4$ that is closest to the point $(0,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the equation of the given line in slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y+x & =-4 \\ y & =-x-4\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the equation of the line that's perpendicular to $y=-x-4$ and passes through the point $(0,2).$

 The given line has a slope of $-1,$ so our perpendicular line must have a slope of $1.$

Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the perpendicular line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-2 & =1(x-0) \\ y-2 & =x \\ y & =x+2\end{aligned}
$$

We now find the point where the two lines intersect. To do this, we solve the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=x+2 \\ y=-x-4\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this system by putting the two equations equal to one another and solving for $x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2 & =-x-4 \\ x+x & =-4-2 \\ 2x & =-6 \\ x & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=-3$ into either of the two equations gives $y=-1.$ So, our solution is $x=-3$ and $y=-1.$ So, the lines intersect at the point $(-3,-1).$

Therefore, we conclude that the point on the line $y+x=-4$ that is closest to the point $(0,2)$ is  $(-3,-1).$

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =\frac{3}{2}(x-2) \\ y-1 & =\frac{3}{2}x-3 \\ y & =\frac{3}{2}x-2\end{aligned}
$$

We now find the point where the two lines intersect. To do this, we solve the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=\frac{3}{2}x-2 \\ y=-\frac{2}{3}x-2\end{aligned}

$$

Find the point on the line $3y+2x=3$ that is closest to the point $(3,5).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the equation of the given line in slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}3y+2x & =3 \\ 3y & =-2x+3 \\ y & =-\frac{2}{3}x+1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the equation of the line that's perpendicular to $y=-\frac{2}{3}x+1$ and passes through the point $(3,5).$

The given line has a slope of $-\frac{2}{3},$ so our perpendicular line must have a slope of $\frac{3}{2}.$

Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the perpendicular line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-5 & =\frac{3}{2}(x-3) \\ y & =\frac{3}{2}x-\frac{9}{2}+5 \\ y & =\frac{3}{2}x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We now find the point where the two lines intersect. To do this, we solve the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=-\frac{2}{3}x+1 \\ y=\frac{3}{2}x+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this system by putting the two equations equal to one another and solving for $x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{3}x+1 & =\frac{3}{2}x+\frac{1}{2} \\ -\frac{2}{3}x-\frac{3}{2}x & =\frac{1}{2}-1 \\ -\frac{13}{6}x & =-\frac{1}{2} \\ x & =\frac{3}{13}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{3}{13}$ into either of the two equations gives $y=\frac{11}{13}.$ So, our solution is $x=\frac{3}{13}$ and $y=\frac{11}{13}.$ So, the lines intersect at the point $(\frac{3}{13},\frac{11}{13}).$

Therefore, we conclude that the point on the line  $3y+2x=3$ that is closest to the point $(3,5)$ is  $(\frac{3}{13},\frac{11}{13}).$

questions.problem: Find the shortest distance between the point $(1,-5)$ and the line $y=-\frac{3}{2}x+3.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's draw a diagram describing our situation.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13934287/assets/3a4bbfd80480fe3fcc778a490514d27d65d83abf77ca1752e4203d9b3185b618.png)

First, we find the equation of the line that's perpendicular to $y=-\frac{3}{2}x+3$ and passes through the point $(1,-5).$

The given line has a slope of $-\frac{3}{2},$ so our perpendicular line must have a slope of $\frac{2}{3}.$

Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the perpendicular line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y+5 & =\frac{2}{3}(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{2}{3}x-\frac{2}{3}-5 \\ y & =\frac{2}{3}x-\frac{17}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We now find the point where the two lines intersect. To do this, we solve the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=-\frac{3}{2}x+3 \\ y=\frac{2}{3}x-\frac{17}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this system by putting the two equations equal to one another and solving for $x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}x+3 & =\frac{2}{3}x-\frac{17}{3} \\ -\frac{3}{2}x-\frac{2}{3}x & =-\frac{17}{3}-3 \\ -\frac{13}{6}x & =-\frac{26}{3} \\ x & =-\frac{26}{3}\cdot (-\frac{6}{13}) \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=4$ into either of the two equations gives $y=-3.$ So, our solution is $x=4$ and $y=-3.$ Therefore, the lines intersect at the point $(4,-3).$

Finally, we find the distance $d$ between the points $(1,-5)$ and $(4,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{({x}_{2}-{x}_{1})^{2}+({y}_{2}-{y}_{1})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(4-1)^{2}+(-3+5)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+4} \\  & =\sqrt{13}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the shortest distance between the point $(1,-5)$ and the line $y=-\frac{3}{2}x+3$ is $\sqrt{13}.$

\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y+3 & =1(x+1) \\ y+3 & =x+1 \\ y & =x-2\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}-x+2 & =x-2 \\ -x-x & =-2-2 \\ -2x & =-4 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}

$$

questions.problem: Find the shortest distance between the point $(-5,3)$ and the line $2y+5x=10.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the equation of the given line in slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}2y+5x & =10 \\ 2y & =-5x+10 \\ y & =-\frac{5}{2}x+5\end{aligned}
$$

Let's draw a diagram describing our situation.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13934287/assets/8c4238a00b775d4db828651ae2691596bfadafcdc748494cc957bad1cb1b6b91.png)

Next, we find the equation of the line that's perpendicular to $y=-\frac{5}{2}x+5$ and passes through the point $(-5,3).$

The given line has a slope of $-\frac{5}{2},$ so our perpendicular line must have a slope of $\frac{2}{5}.$

Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the perpendicular line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-3 & =\frac{2}{5}(x+5) \\ y-3 & =\frac{2}{5}x+2 \\ y & =\frac{2}{5}x+5\end{aligned}
$$

We now find the point where the two lines intersect. To do this, we solve the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=-\frac{5}{2}x+5 \\ y=\frac{2}{5}x+5\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this system by putting the two equations equal to one another and solving for $x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{2}x+5 & =\frac{2}{5}x+5 \\ -\frac{5}{2}x-\frac{2}{5}x & =0 \\ \frac{29}{10}x & =0 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=0$ into either of the two equations gives $y=5.$ So, our solution is $x=0$ and $y=5.$ So, the lines intersect at the point $(0,5).$

Finally, we find the distance $d$ between the points $(-5,3)$ and $(0,5):$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{({x}_{2}-{x}_{1})^{2}+({y}_{2}-{y}_{1})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(0-(-5))}^{2}+(5-3)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25+4} \\  & =\sqrt{29}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the shortest distance between the point $(-5,3)$ and the line $2y+5x=10$ is $\sqrt{29}.$

\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-5 & =-(x+1) \\ y & =-x-1+5 \\ y & =-x+4\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}x-2 & =-x+4 \\ x+x & =4+2 \\ 2x & =6 \\ x & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=3$ into either of the two equations gives $y=1.$ So, our solution is $x=3$ and $y=1.$ Therefore, the lines intersect at the point $(3,1).$

Finally, we find the distance $d$ between the points $(-1,5)$ and $(3,1):$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Point on a Line That Is Closest to a Given Point
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13934287/assets/c48fc163b3c9543dcfdd03b20882f0d2a19747672c6b1db2a42a683f0014fe25.png)

 

Find the point on the line $y-x=4$ that is closest to the point $(3,3).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the equation of the given line in slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-x & =4 \\ y & =x+4\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the equation of the line that is perpendicular to $y =  x + 4$ and passes through the point $(3,3).$ 

The given line has a slope of $1,$ so our perpendicular line must have a slope of $-1.$

Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the perpendicular line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-3 & =-1(x-3) \\ y-3 & =-x+3 \\ y & =-x+6\end{aligned}
$$

We now find the point where the two lines intersect. To do this, we solve the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=x+4 \\ y=-x+6\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this system by putting the two equations equal to one another and solving for $x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x+4 & =-x+6 \\ x+x & =6-4 \\ 2x & =2 \\ x & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=1$ into either of the two equations gives $y=5.$ So, our solution is $x=1$ and $y=5.$ Consequently, the lines intersect at the point $(1,5).$

Therefore, we conclude that the point on the line $y-x= 4$ that is closest to the point $(3,3)$ is  $(1,5).$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Distance Between a Point and a Line
canonical_examples.problem: Find the shortest distance between the point $(1,3)$ and the line $y=\dfrac{1}{2}x -5.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's draw a diagram describing our situation. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13934287/assets/5ccfa3c27c6bb2759ffc37c73b3640583fa962ee79f47b21f02ac0c1d9164b00.png)

 

First, we find the equation of the line that is perpendicular to $y=\dfrac{1}{2}x - 5$ and passes through the point $(1,3).$ 

The given line has a slope of $\dfrac{1}{2},$ so our perpendicular line must have a slope of $-2.$

Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the perpendicular line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-3 & =-2(x-1) \\ y-3 & =-2x+2 \\ y & =-2x+5\end{aligned}
$$

We now find the point where the two lines intersect. To do this, we solve the following system of equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=\frac{1}{2}x-5 \\ y=-2x+5\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this system by setting the two equations equal and solving for $x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}x-5 & =-2x+5 \\ \frac{1}{2}x+2x & =5+5 \\ \frac{5}{2}x & =10 \\ x & =10\cdot \frac{2}{5} \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=4$ into either of the two equations gives $y=-3.$ So, our solution is $x=4$ and $y=-3.$ Consequently, the lines intersect at the point $\left( 4,-3\right).$

Finally, we find the distance $d$ between the points $(1,3)$ and $\left( 4, -3 \right)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{({x}_{2}-{x}_{1})^{2}+({y}_{2}-{y}_{1})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{(4-1)}^{2}+{(-3-3)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+36} \\  & =\sqrt{45} \\  & =\sqrt{9}\sqrt{5} \\  & =3\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the shortest distance between the point $(1,3)$ and the line $y=\dfrac{1}{2}x -5$ is $3 \sqrt{5}.$
